Topic Tree

Myth Check Why Convincing Myths Survive the Facts Myths and misconceptions are not simply foolish beliefs held by poorly informed people. They are ordinary products of human memory, reasoning and social life. A myth is usually a widely shared explanatory story or claim; a misconception is an inaccurate understanding held by an individual or group. 13 pages
Read more
Belief Psychology Why Repeated Claims Start Feeling True Familiarity, memory gaps, emotion, and social identity can make an unsupported claim feel more credible than it is.
Read more
False Consensus When One Repeated Voice Sounds Like a Crowd Repeated messages from one source can resemble broad agreement when reposts, recommendations, and attribution hide their common origin.
Read more
Source Memory When the Claim Outlives Its Warning A claim may remain familiar after its warning, correction, or unreliable source has faded from memory.
Read more
Debunking Do Corrections Really Make Myths Stronger? Corrections usually reduce false belief, while genuine backfire effects are far less common than popular accounts suggest.
Read more
Better Corrections What Makes a Myth Correction Stick? The strongest corrections lead with the truth, identify the error clearly and replace the myth with a memorable explanation.
Read more
Facts and Votes Why Corrected Facts May Not Change Votes People may accept a factual correction yet keep the same political preference because voting also reflects identity, values and trust.
Read more
Health Myths When Health Myths Change Real Decisions Vaccine scares, antibiotic misconceptions, and brain myths show how memorable errors can shape treatment choices and public trust.
Read more
MMR and Autism How a Retracted MMR Claim Kept Spreading A small retracted case series seeded an autism scare that persisted despite large studies finding no increased risk from MMR vaccination.
Read more
Antibiotic Myths Why Antibiotics Do Not Cure Colds and Flu Antibiotics target bacteria rather than viruses, so unnecessary use adds side effects and resistance without treating colds or flu.
Read more
Verify Claims How to Check a Claim Before Sharing Tracing a claim to its origin, checking context, and reading laterally can expose errors that polished presentation conceals.
Read more
Check Studies Does the Study Really Support the Headline? A headline may exaggerate a study by confusing association with causation, ignoring uncertainty or extending results beyond the people tested.
Read more
Verify Media Is That Viral Photo or Video Genuine? Reverse searches, keyframes, landmarks and original uploads can reveal when genuine media has been altered or placed in the wrong context.
